BLACK_AND_WHITE.textHTML:
Black-and-white thinking is a cognitive distortion where we perceive the world in extremes: either perfect or terrible, people are either all good or all bad. This perspective prevents us from noticing the richness of shades and nuances, making the picture too simplified. Ultimately, it limits our view of reality and narrows the range of possible solutions.

This distortion shows up in categorical judgments of ourselves and others, such as “I always fail” or “he is constantly making mistakes.” It can affect any area of life—work, relationships, events, beliefs, our achievements, and our mistakes.

This way of thinking can lead to increased stress, anxiety, low mood, feelings of loneliness, and difficulties in relationships. That’s why it’s important to learn to notice these thoughts and develop a more flexible and realistic outlook. This helps you handle situations better and make more balanced decisions.
BLACK_AND_WHITE.dialogSummary: In this dialogue, Character 1 is thinking in an “all-or-nothing” style: because of one failed exam, they conclude they are completely incapable, without considering the difficulty of the exam or the lack of preparation time.
dialog: I failed the exam, which means I’m hopeless.
The exam was really difficult, and you had very little time to prepare.
It doesn’t matter. If others managed it and I didn’t, it means I’m not smart enough.

CATASTROPHIZATION.textHTML:
Catastrophizing is a cognitive distortion where we tend to exaggerate the significance and consequences of unpleasant events, imagining them to be much worse than they actually are. In these moments, we may feel intense anxiety, fear, and tension that do not reflect the real picture.

Catastrophizing can manifest as the belief that one failure in one area of life will lead to total failure in everything. This can cause intense worry about the future, an overreaction to criticism or rejection, and can undermine self-confidence.

This thinking style can worsen your emotional state, increase anxiety and stress, and lower your self-esteem and belief in your own abilities. It’s important to learn to notice these thoughts and gradually develop a calmer, more realistic view of what’s happening—this helps reduce anxiety and feel more resilient in the face of difficulties.
CATASTROPHIZATION.dialogSummary: In this dialogue, Character 1 is catastrophizing after being rejected in a job interview, believing they will never find work again. They aren’t considering the possibility of continuing the search and adjusting their expectations, which could help them move forward more calmly and confidently.
dialog: I was rejected at the interview. That’s it—now I’ll never find a job and I'll be without work forever.
But you sent your resume to several other vacancies, right?
Yes, but what’s the point? If they didn’t take me here, it means nobody wants me. All my efforts are just pointless.
Such a harsh conclusion can only increase your distress. Perhaps it’s worth giving yourself some time, reassessing your expectations, and continuing the search.
But how can I not think about the failure? It feels like proof that I won’t find a place anywhere and all my plans are falling apart.

COMMON.textHTML:
Overgeneralization is a cognitive distortion where we make broad conclusions based on limited facts or single instances. For example, after receiving one piece of negative feedback at work, you might decide you are completely incompetent, ignoring your own successes and positive results.

A typical situation is being late for a meeting. Instead of calmly analyzing the reasons, we tell ourselves, “I’m always late” or “I never arrive on time,” forgetting the many times we arrived exactly on schedule.

This way of thinking undermines self-esteem, increases pessimism and anxiety, and can fuel depressive thoughts. It is helpful to notice such generalizations and replace them with more balanced and realistic assessments of the specific situation.
COMMON.dialogSummary: Character 1 overgeneralizes from a single instance of being late, attributing chronic disorganization to themselves. Character 2 gently brings the focus back to the facts, reminding them of times they were punctual and suggesting they look at the situation more specifically.
dialog: I can’t believe it, I’m late again. It seems like I’m always late and have no time management skills at all.
Wait, don’t jump to conclusions. Remember how many times you’ve been on time. One instance of being late doesn’t make you chronically unpunctual.
But it’s been happening more often lately. I feel like I’ve lost control.

Let’s look at the facts. Being late once or even twice isn’t a personality trait. External circumstances might have been at play. We can look into the reasons and think about what might help next time.

DISCVAL.textHTML:
Discounting the positive is a cognitive distortion where we tend to downplay the significance of good events, successes, and achievements. In these moments, we focus on flaws or difficulties as if the good things simply don’t exist or “don’t count,” even when they are important and well-deserved results.

This can manifest in any area of life: work, relationships, health, studies, or personal achievements. For example, a person receives well-deserved recognition but, instead of feeling joy, thinks only about their mistakes. Or, upon hearing a compliment, they dismiss it by saying, “it was nothing special” or “I just got lucky.”

Discounting the positive can undermine self-confidence, increase dissatisfaction, and contribute to the formation of depressive thoughts. It’s important to learn to notice and accept the good as attentively as we notice difficulties, and to allow ourselves to enjoy our own successes, even small ones.
DISCVAL.dialogSummary: Character 1 receives a promotion but discounts this success by focusing on the upcoming challenges. Character 2 gently reminds them of the importance of the achievement and supports them, emphasizing the significance of this step in their career.
dialog: I got promoted; now I’ll be leading new projects.
That’s wonderful news, congratulations! What kind of projects will you be leading?
The projects are difficult, and there will be a lot of work. I feel like they’ve just piled more responsibilities on me.
It certainly can be a challenge, but don’t forget that you weren’t chosen by chance. You’ve reached an important milestone, and this is a great opportunity to grow and show what you can do.

DUE.textHTML:
“Should” statements are a cognitive distortion where we are convinced that everything must happen exactly as we expect. When reality doesn’t match our expectations, we may perceive it as unfair or a mistake. In this state, we cling to our expectations and demands, leaving almost no room for flexibility or an objective view of the situation.

For example, one might think, “I must get this job because I prepared so thoroughly.” However, even with great effort, external factors can influence the outcome, including the competitiveness of the position and other strong candidates.

This way of thinking can cause intense disappointment, irritation, and a sense of injustice, negatively affecting your emotional state and relationships with others. It is helpful to learn to notice these attitudes and develop a more flexible approach to outcomes, accepting that different results are possible.
DUE.dialogSummary: Character 1 demonstrates “should” statements, believing they must work without weekends to achieve success, based on other people’s stories. Character 2 helps them see the bigger picture, reminding them that everyone has their own path and that a balance between work and rest can be a healthier and more effective approach.
dialog: I must work every day without weekends; otherwise, I’ll never succeed.
Why did you come to that conclusion? What made you think that?
I’ve read stories of successful people. They all worked hard and almost never rested.

Everyone has their own path. For some, that lifestyle really works, but for others, a healthy balance is more helpful. It’s important to understand that rest is also necessary—it helps you maintain energy and move toward your goals sustainably.

EMO.textHTML:
The cognitive distortion known as “emotional reasoning” occurs when we make decisions based solely on our current feelings rather than on logic and facts. In these moments, emotions feel like the ultimate proof that a situation is exactly as we feel it is, even if that isn’t objectively true.

For example, a person might decline a meeting with friends because they feel sad and believe it won’t change anything. But in reality, socializing and support could actually help improve their mood and restore their energy.

Emotions are important, but relying solely on them can lead to mistaken conclusions and decisions. It is helpful to pay attention not only to your feelings but also to the facts, so you can make more balanced and stable decisions.
EMO.dialogSummary: In this dialogue, Character 1 makes a decision based entirely on sadness and insecurity, declining a date. Character 2 gently helps them see the bigger picture and suggests that the actual experience might be much more pleasant than their current mood suggests.
dialog: I don’t want to go on a date. I’m in a bad mood.
But you liked this person. Maybe give yourself a chance and see how it goes?
I feel insecure and awkward. I’m sure I’ll just ruin everything.
You can’t know in advance. The meeting could turn out to be pleasant and supportive, and you might end up feeling much better than you do now.

FILTER.textHTML:
Mental filtering is a cognitive distortion where we focus primarily on negative moments and pay almost no attention to the positive ones. For example, after an unsuccessful interview, a person might focus solely on the rejection, forgetting the valuable experience and new knowledge that will help them in the future.

This approach can lead to feelings of dissatisfaction and lower your mood, even when there is plenty of good in your life. Often, mental filtering goes hand in hand with other distortions, such as black-and-white thinking or discounting the positive.

To gradually overcome mental filtering, it is helpful to practice noticing positive moments, asking yourself supportive questions, and reminding yourself of your successes and strengths.
FILTER.dialogSummary: In this dialogue, Character 1 is fixated on a single piece of negative feedback, failing to notice the positive aspects of their work. Character 2 helps them see the bigger picture and focus on the facts that confirm their successes and efforts.
dialog: I got some negative feedback at work. I feel like a failure.
But you’ve had so many positive reviews and achievements. It feels like you’re putting too much weight on one negative moment.
Yes, but this feedback feels like the most important thing. It’s as if it cancels out all my successes.

Right now, you’re only seeing the negative side of the situation and missing the rest of the facts. That’s mental filtering. Try to look at the bigger picture and remember the good things you’ve accomplished.

LABEL.textHTML:
Labeling is a cognitive distortion where we give people or situations categorical and oversimplified assessments based on limited observations. As a result, we stop noticing other sides of a person or an event, and our perception becomes distorted.

For example, someone might call another person “strange” or “unworthy” based solely on their appearance or a single episode of behavior. Similarly, when we label ourselves—for instance, calling ourselves “bad” or “incompetent”—we ignore our strengths, successes, and true qualities.

When we learn to notice this distortion, it becomes easier to see people and ourselves more fully and fairly, without jumping to conclusions.
LABEL.dialogSummary: Character 1 concludes that a man is a “bad father” after seeing a single episode of him shouting at his children. Character 2 offers a more balanced perspective, reminding them that one observation isn’t enough and that people can behave differently in different situations.
dialog: I saw that man shouting at his kids in the park. He’s definitely a bad father.
It’s hard to judge based on just one moment. Maybe he was having a hard day or something happened that threw him off balance.
I would never act like that with my own children. It seems like he just can’t handle being a parent.
Categorical conclusions can be misleading. People react differently in stressful situations, and on another day, he might be a very caring and attentive father.

MAYBE.textHTML:
The “should have” distortion occurs when we mentally revisit past events and imagine ideal alternatives that were actually unavailable in reality. We start thinking in terms of “what if” and create fantasies about how things could have turned out differently.

Sometimes this shows up in communication: we tell ourselves or others that things should have been done differently, without considering the actual circumstances at the time.

This perspective often leads to feelings of guilt, regret, and dissatisfaction, as we compare reality to unattainable, ideal scenarios. It is helpful to remember that the past cannot be changed, but we can choose what to do next.
MAYBE.dialogSummary: In this dialogue, Character 1 views an exam through the lens of “what should have been,” blaming themselves and the circumstances. Character 2 helps gently shift the focus back to the present and the future, reminding them that the most important thing is the steps they can take now.
dialog: I failed the exam. I should have studied more.
But you worked every day and did your absolute best. You acted within the circumstances you had.
Yes, but I would have studied more if I didn’t have to work.
You can’t change the past. Right now, it’s more important to think about how to support yourself and manage your time better in the future.

MORE_MINE.textHTML:
The “magnification and minimization” distortion occurs when we look at events in an overly one-sided way, missing the nuances and details. With magnification, negative moments seem huge and significant, as if seen through a magnifying glass. With minimization, we downplay our strengths, successes, and positive events, as if they don’t matter.

For example, a person might consider themselves a failure due to small mistakes while failing to notice their own achievements and the efforts that led them to success.

This approach can negatively impact self-esteem and relationships, as the perception of reality becomes distorted. It is helpful to learn to notice the balance: seeing both the mistakes and the strengths, and valuing the contributions you are already making.
MORE_MINE.dialogSummary: In this dialogue, Character 1 exaggerates their awkwardness during an interview, while Character 2 gently helps them refocus on their strengths and abilities, supporting a more balanced view.
dialog: I’m so nervous about the interview tomorrow. I always stumble over my words.
It sounds like you’re magnifying your awkwardness right now. You’re much more capable than you think.
But I often lose my train of thought and forget what I wanted to say.
You have important strengths: you know how to adapt quickly and find solutions. That is a truly valuable quality for an interview.
Really? Thanks, I’ll try to keep that in mind.

READ.textHTML:
The cognitive distortion known as “mind reading” occurs when we assume we know what others are thinking or feeling without any real evidence. We rely on guesswork rather than facts, and often find ourselves trapped by mistaken conclusions.

For example, you might decide that someone is being unkind to you because of their behavior, when in reality, it might be related to their mood, their worries, or their fatigue. It can also work the other way—we might think someone understands our intentions or feelings even though we haven’t expressed them directly.

When we notice this distortion, it becomes easier to avoid incorrect assumptions and build more honest, open communication based on facts rather than guesswork.
READ.dialogSummary: In this dialogue, Character 1 draws a conclusion about a colleague’s mood based on their own assumptions. Character 2 gently reminds them that without a direct conversation, one cannot be certain of another person’s thoughts and feelings.
dialog: Maria didn’t say hello to me in the office yesterday. She’s probably angry with me because I was late for the meeting.
Are you sure? Maybe she was just busy or didn’t notice you. Have you tried asking her?
No, I didn’t ask. But something tells me that’s exactly what it is.
We can’t be sure what someone else is thinking without talking to them. She might have had her own reasons that have nothing to do with you.

RESPONSE.textHTML:
Personalization is a cognitive distortion where we perceive events as being directed personally against us, even when there is no real basis for it. It’s as if we place ourselves at the center of a situation and take things personally that may have nothing to do with us.

For example, if someone doesn’t say hello, you might decide they are intentionally ignoring you or dislike you. In doing so, you might miss the fact that they could be dealing with their own worries, be in a rush, or simply be distracted. Personalization also shows up when we believe that any negative event is a reflection of our own flaws, ignoring external circumstances.
RESPONSE.dialogSummary: Character 1 perceives a job rejection as proof of their incompetence. Character 2 gently reminds them that the result could depend on many factors and does not define their personality or abilities.
dialog: I didn’t pass the interview. I guess I’m just not capable of handling important tasks.
That doesn’t have to be the case. Perhaps the company had specific requirements or candidates who were a better fit for that particular role.
But every time something important happens, I fail. It seems like I’m just not good enough.

Mistakes and rejections are a normal part of the journey. They don’t mean there is something wrong with you. It’s important to consider different factors and not link every situation solely to your worth or abilities.
